''Officers” Versus 'Employees.” Although the Buckley opinion 
establishes the exclusivity of the Article II appointments protocols for officers 
of the United States,” its definition of “officer” is less than pellucid. The closest 
the opinion comes to announcing a standard is its insistence that the 
performance of a significant governmental duty exercised pursuant to a public 
law” may be assigned only to an “officer.” Conversely, the Court indicates that 
this class of duties does not include powers that operate “only in aid of those 
functions that Congress may carry out by itself, or in an area sufficiently 
removed from the administration and enforcement of the public law.” Thus, for 
example, powers of information gathering or dissemination that Congress 
might delegate to one of its own committees,” do not trigger “officer” status.
Freytag v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 501 U.S. 868 (1991), applied 
the Buckley formulation to hold that special trial judges of the U.S. Tax Court 
were “officers of the United States.” The Court observed:
The office of special trial judge is “established by Law,” Art. II, § 2, cl.
2, and the duties, salary, and means of appointment for that office 
are specified by statute. These characteristics distinguish special 
trial judges from special masters, who are hired by Article III courts 
on a temporary, episodic basis, whose positions are not estabhshed 
by law, and whose duties and functions are not delineated in a 
statute. Furthermore, special trial judges perform more than 
ministerial tasks. They take testimony, conduct trials, rule on the 
admissibihty of evidence, and have the power to enforce compliance 
with discovery orders. In the course of carrying out these important 
functions, the special trial judges exercise significant discretion.
Id. at 881-82. Moreover, the Court stressed, “the Chief Judge may assign 
special trial judges to render the decisions of the Tax Court in declaratory 
judgment proceedings and limited-amount tax cases.” In such cases, “special 
trial judges act as inferior officers who exercise independent authority.” Id. 
They thus were officers, and not employees. Freytag did not indicate, however, 
whether any and all of the functions mentioned would alone qualify an 
administrative adjudicator as an “officer.”
In Lucia v. S.E.C., 138 S. Ct. 2044 (2018), the Court—without further 
refining the Buckley test—relied on Freytag to hold that Administrative Law 
Judges working for the Securities and Exchange Commission were also 
“officers.” (The general impheations of Lucia for aHministrative adjudication
